newsitem.title: ICELAND: Iceland takes lead in false limbs.
newsitem.headline: Iceland takes lead in false limbs.

text.p: Life was shattered for Dennis Kovacevic, a 15-year-old Bosnian, when his right leg was shattered by a mine.
The teenager, who was raised in a village near Bihac, was walking his bicycle across a field when he trod on the mine, ripping his right leg apart and badly injuring his left.
But unlike the 2,000 civilians each year that are injured or killed by land mines, Dennis had a lucky break.

While he was being treated in a Zagreb hospital in May, he was spotted by a team of prosthetists from Ossur Ltd., an Icelandic firm that is leading a new wave of innovative enterprises from the fish-dominated North Atlantic country.
They were trying out a new process, developed for victims of wars and natural disasters, that enables artificial legs and arms to be fitted on the spot rather than taking the usual four days.

"By that afternoon he was up and running about," Ossur's quality assurance manager, Huld Magnusdottir, told Reuters. "The prosthetists only had an adult ankle with them but Dennis refused to let them take away his new found freedom."

The new process, ICEX, involves soaking a strong, lightweight carbon braid in a pre-impregnated polyurethane resin and wrapping it around the stump of the limb. The material sets quickly, forming a tailor-made sheath or socket that can be fitted with attachments needed for a false limb.
Magnusdottir said the new process was designed primarily for treating casualties in isolated areas in emergency situations.
"You can do it in a very short period of time and you don't need electricity. All you need is a bucket of water so you really can go anywhere and do this," Magnusdottir said.

Ossur, set up in 1971 by prosthetist Ossur Kristensson, first went international in 1990 with a new silicon sock for lining false limbs to stop rubbing against the skin and eliminate the need for straps to keep false limbs in place.
Now the world leader in prosthetics development, Ossur has over the past two years set up centres in California, Britain and Luxembourg and last year exported goods worth $6.5 million.
"People tend to think of Iceland in terms of fish so people are surprised that we are doing things that are totally different," Magnusdottir said.

The Trade Council of Iceland said Ossur was typical of the variety of innovative companies emerging in Iceland, although the economy remains fish-dependent. Last year 54 percent of foreign earnings came from marine products.

Council spokesman Andres Petursson said new companies range from exporting the nation's small, sturdy horses, to music production, led by band members formerly supporting Iceland's own queen of pop, Bjork.

One industry that has become particularly successful in Iceland is computer software. The remote island boasts the highest number of computers per capita in the world, with one in every four people in the population of 265,000 owning a PC. Icelanders are the world's most prolific Internet surfers.
"People are trying to do something different and break away from the reliance on fish," Petursson said.
Some entrepreneurial Icelanders are also looking at the fishing industry, selling on-board weighing equipment and offering to market other countries' fish.
The national carrier Icelandair advertises fish skin wallets for sale in its on-board gift brochure.
"We'll always be dependent on fish as that's our only real area of expertise and we aim to become the world's fishmonger. But Iceland can offer now more than that," said Petursson.
